query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 5 at.% Sn to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures by promoting the formation of a continuous, adherent Sn-containing protective oxide scale that slows down pesting oxidation, while preserving the useful room‐ and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy with demonstrated room-temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) but with inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled Sn addition (near 5 at.%) into the alloy composition during melting/casting.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at high temperatures (targeting 800 °C up to 1200 °C) for 5 hours, with minimal mechanical load during oxidation testing to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, dense tin-containing oxide scale (possibly incorporating SnO2 or interacting with existing oxides) that adheres well to the substrate.
generation.mechanism: Sn addition is expected to alter the oxidation kinetics by enabling a modified oxidation pathway where Sn preferentially oxidizes to form a protective scale that limits oxygen ingress. This may also stabilize certain oxide phases and reduce scale spallation, as evidenced by prior studies on similar alloy systems.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the Sn-modified alloy should exhibit a significantly lower oxide scale growth rate and reduced pesting, while retaining comparable room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which shows inadequate oxygen resistance under high-temperature air exposure (e.g., 5 h at 800 °C).
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 800–1200 °C; Atmosphere: Air; Exposure time: 5 hours; Mechanical loading: negligible during oxidation testing to focus on oxidation behavior; alloy processing conditions similar to the cast state used in prior studies.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Sn concentration and its possible side effects (such as phase stability or unintended changes to mechanical properties) remain uncertain. Further, the exact nature and composition of the protective oxide scale are not fully established in this system.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one of the standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and one with an additional 5 at.% Sn. Subject identically processed samples from both sets to an oxidation test in air at a targeted temperature (e.g., 800 °C) for 5 hours. Post-exposure, assess the oxide scale properties (thickness, continuity, adherence) and perform weight gain measurements. Additionally, evaluate the retention of mechanical properties (room temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength) by standard tensile testing.
measurements: Weight gain per unit area to quantify oxidation rate
Oxide scale thickness and morphology via microscopy (SEM/TEM)
Phase identification and chemical composition of the oxide scale (XRD/EDS)
Mechanical properties (tensile ductility at room temperature and yield strength at 1000 °C) before and after oxidation exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-added alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., similar weight gain and oxide scale spallation) or if its mechanical properties are degraded in comparison to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis that Sn addition improves oxygen resistance while preserving mechanical performance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The research on the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys would suggest (a) that Ge and/or Sn are needed to suppress pest oxidation, and (b) that, when these alloying additions were present individually or simultaneously in the alloys, the spallation of their scales at high temperatures was not suppressed. It is now well established that Ge or Sn has an effect on macrosegregation and can also reduce the liquidus temperature of the alloy. Alloying with Sn can affect the stability of the Nbss but not the alloying with Ge, which can, however, significantly reduce the cracking of the substrate below the scale/substrate interface []. Unfortunately, from the oxidation research on multicomponent Nb-silicide-based alloys, it is not clear whether it was the synergy of Sn or Ge individually or simultaneously with Al, Cr, Si, and Ti that improved oxidation resistance, or whether the presence of oxygen scavenging Hf with/without transition and refractory metals and with some or all of the aforementioned elements was essential for increasing the oxidation resistance.

The encouraging result of the research presented in this paper is that a Ti lean Nb-silicide-based alloy with simultaneous addition of RM (essential for strength and creep [,]), Al, Cr, Ge, Hf and Sn (essential for oxidation resistance [,]) can “match” the high temperature oxidation of the best oxidation resistant Ti rich alloys, some of which are B-containing alloys []. Undeniably, the inferior oxidation performance in the pest regime is a matter of concern, and must be addressed by future alloy development research.

chosen.approach: Alloy additions (Sn/Ge/B) to form protective oxide scales
